title: Coding & Algorithms
description: Coding and algorithms from unplugged games to real programs: sequences and instructions, directions and grids, patterns and loops, debugging, conditionals and events, variables, block-based programming, functions, data structures, searching and sorting, text-based programming in Python, algorithm efficiency, and the ideas of computer science.

lessons.title: First, Next, Last
objectives: Put instructions in the right order
Explain why the order of steps matters
explanation: An algorithm is a set of step-by-step instructions to do something. Brushing your teeth, making a sandwich and getting dressed all follow algorithms!
The order matters. If you put on your shoes before your socks, it doesn't work! Computers follow instructions exactly, in order.
Coding means writing instructions that a computer can follow. Before computers, we can practise by giving instructions to friends or toy robots.

vocabulary.meaning: one step telling what to do
which comes first, next and last

examples: Socks first, then shoes.
Wash hands, then eat.

story.title: Robot Papa
story.text: Ivaan told Papa, "Make me a sandwich!" Papa stood still like a robot. "Instructions, please." Ivaan said, "Put jam on bread." Papa rubbed the jam jar — still closed — on the bread bag! Ivaan giggled. "Open the bag. Take out bread. Open the jar..." Step by step, a perfect sandwich appeared. "Robots need every step!" Ivaan laughed.

lessons.title: Guide the Robot
objectives: Use forward, back, left and right to move on a grid

explanation: A robot on a grid can move forward, move back, turn left and turn right. We can write arrows to show the moves: ⬆️ forward, ⬅️ left, ➡️ right.
To reach a goal, we plan the path: "Forward, forward, turn right, forward." Each square counts as one step.
If the robot goes the wrong way, we look at our instructions to find the mistake. Finding and fixing mistakes is called debugging.

lessons.title: Repeat 3 Times
objectives: Find repeating patterns in instructions
Rewrite repeated steps as a loop
explanation: Sometimes instructions repeat: "clap, clap, clap, clap." Instead of writing it many times, we can say "repeat clap 4 times." This is a loop.
Loops save time and make code shorter. A song chorus that repeats is like a loop.
To draw a square with a robot, you could write: forward, turn, forward, turn, forward, turn, forward, turn. Or simply: repeat 4 times (forward, turn).

vocabulary.meaning: something that happens again and again

Walking around a square: repeat 4 times (walk, turn).

story.text: A wizard had to write the spell "Sparkle!" one hundred times on a scroll. His hand ached after ten. His clever apprentice said, "Write: REPEAT 100 TIMES: Sparkle!" The wizard tried it, and one hundred sparkles burst into the sky at once. "A loop!" he cried. "Why didn't I think of that?"

lessons.title: Be a Bug Hunter
objectives: Find a mistake in a set of instructions
Test, fix and test again
explanation: A bug is a mistake in code that makes it do the wrong thing. Everyone makes bugs — even expert programmers!
To find a bug, go through the instructions one step at a time and check what happens at each step. When something goes wrong, you've found the bug.

A famous story: in 1947, engineers working on the Harvard Mark II computer found a real moth stuck in it and taped it in their logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found". Grace Hopper, a computing pioneer, loved telling this story.

vocabulary.meaning: to try something to see if it works
to check one step at a time

examples: A robot path that turns the wrong way.
A recipe missing "turn on the oven".

story.title: The Moth in the Machine

lessons.title: If It Rains, Take an Umbrella
objectives: Explain if-then-else conditions
Write conditionals for everyday decisions
explanation: Programs make decisions using conditions. "If it is raining, then take an umbrella." The part after "if" is the condition — it is either true or false.
If-then-else gives two choices: "If it is raining, then take an umbrella, else wear sunglasses."
Games use conditions all the time: "If the player touches a coin, then add 1 point." "If lives = 0, then game over."

vocabulary.meaning: something that is true or false
do something only when a condition is true
what to do when the condition is false

examples: If the light is red, stop; else go.
If you are hungry, eat a snack.

lessons.title: Make a Sprite Move
objectives: Use events, motion and loop blocks to animate a character
Create a short interactive program
explanation: Block-based languages, like Scratch (created at MIT and first released in 2007) and ScratchJr, let you snap blocks together like puzzle pieces instead of typing.

A sprite is a character in the program. Event blocks start the code: "when green flag clicked" or "when this sprite clicked". Motion blocks move it; looks blocks change how it appears; sound blocks play sounds.
Combining events, loops and conditions creates interactive stories and games: "When green flag clicked, forever: if touching edge, bounce."

vocabulary.meaning: a character or object in a program
something that starts code, like a click

examples: A cat sprite that meows when clicked.
A fish that swims back and forth forever.

lessons.title: Keeping Score
objectives: Explain what a variable is
Use a variable to keep score in a game
prerequisites: Can build block programs with events and conditions
explanation: A variable is like a labelled box that stores information a program needs to remember — a score, a name, the number of lives.
Variables can change: "set score to 0" at the start, then "change score by 1" each time the player catches a star.
Variables can store numbers, text (called strings) or true/false values (called Booleans, after the mathematician George Boole).

lessons.title: Write It Once, Use It Many Times
objectives: Define and use a function with a parameter
Break a big problem into smaller parts
explanation: A function is a named set of instructions you can use again and again. Instead of writing "draw a square" code many times, you define a function called drawSquare and call it whenever you need a square.
Functions can take inputs called parameters. drawSquare(size) can draw big or small squares depending on the size you give it.
Breaking a big problem into smaller parts — decomposition — is a key skill. A house drawing might use functions for drawSquare, drawTriangle and drawWindow.

vocabulary.meaning: a named, reusable set of instructions
breaking a problem into smaller parts

examples: drawSquare(50) and drawSquare(100).
A "make tea" function used every morning.

lessons.title: Hello, Python
objectives: Write Python programs using print, input, variables and conditions
Use for and while loops
prerequisites: Understands variables, loops and conditions in blocks
explanation: Python is a popular text-based programming language, created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. It is known for being readable.

print("Hello") shows text. name = input("Your name? ") asks the user to type something. if age >= 13: ... elif ...: ... else: ... makes decisions. Indentation (spaces at the start of lines) shows which code belongs inside a block.
for i in range(5): repeats 5 times (i goes 0 to 4). while lives > 0: repeats as long as the condition is true. Careful — a while loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever!

vocabulary.meaning: the rules for writing code in a language

examples: print("Namaste, " + name)

She added it, ran the program, and it asked, "What is 2 + 2?" She typed 4. "Correct!" printed on the screen. One tiny symbol, one big smile.

lessons.title: Find It Fast
objectives: Use lists in Python
Compare linear and binary search, and trace bubble sort
explanation: A list stores many values in order: marks = [72, 85, 90]. Each item has an index starting at 0, so marks[0] is 72.

Linear search checks items one by one. Binary search works only on sorted lists: check the middle; if the target is smaller, search the left half, otherwise the right half. Each step halves the list, so binary search is much faster on big lists — about 20 checks for a million items.

Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbouring items that are in the wrong order until the list is sorted. It is simple but slow for large lists; faster algorithms like merge sort and quicksort are used in practice.

vocabulary.meaning: searching a sorted list by halving it

examples: Finding a word in a dictionary by opening in the middle.
Sorting cards by repeatedly swapping neighbours.

lessons.title: How Fast Is Fast?
objectives: Describe algorithm efficiency using Big O notation
Write and trace a recursive function
explanation: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's running time grows as input size n grows. Linear search is O(n); binary search is O(log n); bubble sort is O(n²); merge sort is O(n log n).
For a million items, O(n²) means around a trillion steps, but O(n log n) only about twenty million. Choosing the right algorithm can matter more than a faster computer.

Recursion is when a function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem, with a base case to stop. Merge sort recursively splits a list in half, sorts each half and merges them — a "divide and conquer" strategy.

vocabulary.meaning: notation describing how running time grows with input size
splitting a problem into smaller subproblems

examples: factorial(n) = n × factorial(n − 1), with factorial(0) = 1.
Merge sort splitting [8,3,5,1] into [8,3] and [5,1].

story.title: The Tower of Hanoi
story.text: A legend tells of priests moving 64 golden discs between three poles, never placing a bigger disc on a smaller one. The recursive solution takes 2⁶⁴ − 1 moves. At one move per second, that would take hundreds of billions of years — far longer than the age of the universe. Some problems are simple to describe but enormous to compute.

lessons.title: Stacks, Graphs and the Limits of Computing
objectives: Choose suitable data structures for problems
Explain the halting problem and ethical issues in algorithms
explanation: Data structures organise data for efficient use. A stack is last-in-first-out (like a pile of plates; used for "undo"). A queue is first-in-first-out (like a ticket line). A dictionary (hash map) looks up values by key quickly. A graph models connections — maps, social networks — and algorithms like Dijkstra's find shortest paths.

In 1936, Alan Turing described an abstract "Turing machine" and proved that no general algorithm can decide, for every program and input, whether it will eventually stop — the halting problem. Some problems are uncomputable.

Algorithms also raise ethical questions: biased training data can lead to unfair decisions in hiring or lending; recommendation algorithms shape what people see. Computer scientists increasingly study fairness, transparency and accountability.

vocabulary.meaning: the proven impossibility of deciding in general whether programs stop

examples: A browser's back button as a stack.
GPS navigation using shortest-path algorithms on a graph.

story.title: Turing's Machine on Paper
story.text: In 1936, before electronic computers existed, 24-year-old Alan Turing imagined a machine with an endless tape, reading and writing symbols by simple rules. With this paper machine, he proved that some questions can never be answered by any algorithm — and laid the foundations of computer science.
